H1.text: Aarav reads how chips are made.

H2.text: First, silicon is cleaned until it is purer than almost anything.

H3.text: Then the factory adds impurity back in. On purpose!

I1.text: Why clean it, just to make it dirty again?

I2.text: Because the right impurity turns silicon into a useful conductor.

L1.text: Think of a class where every student holds hands with four friends.

L2.text: Nobody is free to walk around. Everyone is busy holding hands.

L3.text: That is pure silicon. Each atom has four outer electrons.

L4.text: It shares them with four neighbours. Each shared pair is a covalent bond.

L5.text: Now warm the crystal a little, to room temperature.

L6.text: Heat shakes one bond loose. An electron breaks free and wanders off.

L7.text: It leaves behind an empty spot. We call it a hole.

L8.text: A hole acts like a positive charge.

L9.text: A neighbour's electron hops into the hole.

L10.text: Now the hole has moved one step the other way.

L11.text: Like an empty seat moving down a cinema row as people shift.

P1.text: Every free electron made this way leaves exactly one hole.

P2.text: So in pure silicon, electrons and holes are always equal in number.

P3.text: We write n e equals n h equals n i.

P4.text: n i is the intrinsic carrier concentration. Intrinsic means pure, with nothing added.

P5.text: For silicon at room temperature, n i is tiny.

P5b.text: About one point five times ten to the sixteen per cubic metre.

P6.text: That sounds big. But a cubic metre of silicon has far more atoms.

P6b.text: Five times ten to the twenty eight of them.

P7.text: So only about one atom in three trillion frees an electron.

P7b.text: That is why pure silicon is a poor conductor.

D1.text: Now we add impurity. This is called doping.

D2.text: Silicon with impurity added is an extrinsic semiconductor.

D3.text: First, add a few arsenic atoms.

D4.text: Arsenic is pentavalent. That means it has five outer electrons.

D5.text: Four of them join bonds with silicon. The fifth one has no partner.

D6.text: A tiny push, about point zero five electron volts, sets it free.

D7.text: Arsenic donates an electron, so it is called a donor.

D8.text: Now electrons far outnumber holes. This is n-type. Electrons are the majority carriers.

D10.text: Indium is trivalent. It has only three outer electrons.

D11.text: One bond is left with a missing electron. That is a ready-made hole.

D12.text: Indium accepts an electron to fill it, so it is called an acceptor.

D13.text: Now holes are the majority. This is p-type. Electrons become the minority.

T1.text: A pinch of impurity brings a flood of carriers.

B1.text: Let's see it on the breadboard.

B2.text: A battery drives current through a small block of silicon.

B3.text: Pure silicon first. The current on the scope is tiny.

B4.text: Now dope it. One arsenic atom for every ten million silicon atoms.

B5.text: Watch the scope jump. Free electrons pour into the circuit.

B6.text: Look at the readout. Electrons went up hugely.

B7.text: But holes went down. Why would holes drop?

M2.text: More free electrons means more of them fall into holes and fill them.

M3.text: This filling is called recombination. So the holes get fewer.

M4.text: The rule is n e times n h equals n i squared.

M5.text: It is called the mass action law. It holds in pure and doped crystals alike.

W1.text: Worked example. Our doped silicon block.

W2.text: Silicon has five times ten to the twenty eight atoms per cubic metre.

W3.text: One arsenic per ten million gives five times ten to the twenty one donors.

W4.text: Each donor gives one electron. So n e is five times ten to the twenty one.

W5.text: Holes: n h equals n i squared divided by n e.

W6.text: Square one point five times ten to the sixteen.

W6b.text: That gives two point two five times ten to the thirty two.

W7.text: Divide by five times ten to the twenty one.

W7b.text: n h is four point five times ten to the ten.

W8.text: Electrons now beat holes by about a hundred billion to one.

X2.text: Many students say n-type silicon is negatively charged. It is not.

X3.text: Each extra electron leaves behind a fixed positive arsenic ion. The crystal stays neutral.

X4.text: Where is this asked? PUC, CBSE and ISC boards ask about doping and carriers.

X5.text: JEE Main uses the mass action law, as in July twenty twenty one.

Q1.text: Try this. Germanium has n i of two point four times ten to the nineteen. It is doped with indium, four point eight times ten to the twenty one per cubic metre. Which is correct?

A1.text: A. It is p-type, with electrons at one point two times ten to the seventeen.

A2.text: Indium is trivalent, an acceptor. So holes are the majority, and it is p-type.

A3.text: n h is about equal to the acceptor count, four point eight times ten to the twenty one.

A4.text: n e is n i squared over n h. That gives one point two times ten to the seventeen.
